title: How life looked: 1825, 1925, 2025
sub: Cities, homes, living, dress, mobility and hygiene, set side by side at three dates
lede: The question is whether life looked much the same in 1925 as in 1825, and how far today's look is the product of the last hundred years. Each table puts what I could count at three dates, and says where I found nothing.
asof: Figures current to 27 October 2026. Most series are the nearest year available, named in each cell.

domains.intro: What was worn, what it was made of, and how much cloth the world now produces.

rows.label: About 1925

rows.label: About 1925

rows.label: About 2025

domains.solid: How solid The 1820s and 1920s rows come from Wikipedia's fashion articles, which describe Western dress only. I did not fetch a source describing present-day dress, so the 2025 cells for the silhouette rows are empty on purpose. The fibre figures are from an industry report summarized by a trade publication. The Wikipedia list dates polyester to 1953 and nylon to 1931, which conflicts with the dates in its own text; I used the text.

domains.title: Mobility
domains.intro: How long it took to cross the Atlantic, how many motor vehicles there were, and how many people fly.

rows.text: Sailing packets averaged 23 days eastbound and 40 days westbound (the years are not stated). The fastest passages were 15 d 16 h east (1823) and 15 d 23 h west (1830). Steam: the Great Western took 15 d 12 h west in 1838.
rows.label: About 1825

rows.text: Mauretania eastbound, August 1924: 5 d 1 h 49 min. Alcock and Brown flew it in 16 h 12 min in June 1919; Lindbergh in 33.5 h in May 1927.
rows.label: About 1925

rows.text: Fastest subsonic airliner crossing, 4 h 56 min, 8–9 February 2020, helped by a tailwind. Concorde was scheduled at about 3 h 15 min westbound. I found no sourced typical time today.
rows.label: About 2025

rows.text: United States: about 20.1 million registered in 1925, 17.5 million of them cars. Vehicles per 1,000 people: 86.8 in 1920 and 217.3 in 1930.
rows.label: About 1925

rows.text: About 1.55 billion motor vehicles in use worldwide in 2023. I found no world figure for 1925.
rows.label: About 2025

rows.text: No scheduled airplane passenger service across the Atlantic until 1939; the Graf Zeppelin airship began scheduled crossings in 1931.
rows.label: About 1925

rows.text: 4.7 billion passengers on scheduled services in 2024, 37.4 million departures.
rows.label: About 2025

The vehicle figures for the United States are from earlier reading and I could not recover their links, so they are not listed under sources. The 2024 air figures are preliminary and come from ICAO.

domains.intro: Life expectancy, the death of children, and clean water, sanitation and handwashing.

rows.text: About 29 at the beginning of the 19th century.
rows.label: About 1825

rows.text: 31–32 in 1900 and 45.7–48 in 1950. No figure for 1925 itself.
rows.label: About 1925

rows.text: About one-quarter in 1950. No figure for 1925.
rows.label: About 1925

rows.text: 2.1 billion people, 1 in 4, lacked it; 106 million drank untreated surface water.
rows.label: About 2025

rows.label: About 2025

domains.solid: How solid The life expectancy figures are for the world and rest on historical reconstructions, which the Wikipedia page itself treats with caution; the 1900 figure differs between sources. The water, sanitation and hygiene figures are the WHO and UNICEF's 2025 report, a primary source. I found no matching world figures for 1825 or 1925.

patterns.h3: In the United States, the premise does not hold as stated
p: By 1925 half of US households had electric power, and the car reached the same share the next year (1926). Radio had passed 10 percent. The 1925 hemline also differs sharply from the 1820s silhouette. Atlantic crossings had fallen from 23–40 days to about 5. I have household data only for the United States, so I cannot say the same of Europe; the dress and crossing rows cover Western fashion and the North Atlantic.

patterns.h3: For much of the world it holds better
p: Around 1920 the urban share was about 10 percent in both Africa and Asia, and it reached about 43 and 46 percent by 2016. In 2000, 2 in 10 people still lacked electricity and about half lacked clean cooking fuels. For these regions the large visible shift came after 1925.

patterns.h3: The largest change in the second century is in health and numbers, not in objects
p: Life expectancy was about 29 in the early 1800s and 31–32 in 1900, then 72.6–73.2 in 2019–2020. Child deaths before 15 fell from about a quarter in 1950 to 4% in 2020. This is the change a photograph of 1925 would not show.

patterns.h3: Both centuries saw the speed of the journey fall by a large factor, in different ways
p: From the 40-day westbound packet to the 1924 Mauretania, about 5 days, the time fell roughly eightfold. From 1924 to the fastest 2020 airliner crossing, about 25-fold. The second figure compares a ship with an aircraft, so it measures a change of method as much as of speed.

My reading: 'visually similar by 1925' is better described as 'the shape of modern household life was in place in the United States by 1925, and reached much of the rest of the world after it'. What changed after 1925 was how many people shared it, how long they lived, and how fast and far they could travel.

limits: The three snapshot dates are loose. Many sources give 1900, 1920, 1950 or 2016 instead of 1825, 1925 and 2025, and each cell names the year it uses.
The household technology series is for the United States only. I found no matching world series for the same machines.
The 1825 column is the thinnest. For most rows I did not find a figure for that date, and I have left it blank rather than estimate.
Dress is described for Western fashion only and I have no 2025 description at all.
Wikipedia and OWID pages were read through a summarizing tool, and a few values come from chart data files rather than page text. Check the figures against the originals before relying on them.
A statement of appearance, such as a skirt or a skyline, cannot be reduced to a figure. These tables show what can be counted, not how life felt.

footer: Several statements are general knowledge, not tied to a fetched source: that there was no household electric supply and no motor vehicle in 1825. The ratios of crossing times (about eightfold and about 25-fold), the idea that the shape of household life was in place by 1925, and the reading of the regional urban shares are my own arithmetic or reading. Two groups of figures came from earlier fetches whose links I could not recover: the US vehicle registrations and vehicles per 1,000 people, and the 1800–2016 regional urban shares come from an OWID chart (see the sources). The vehicle figures are not in the source list.
